frequency_question: How often do structural frictions (legal challenges, administrative rule-making delays, institutional vetoes) successfully halt or delay an announced executive trade restriction before its effective date?
membership_rule: Includes major unilateral tariff proclamations or quota enactments via executive order or emergency powers where implementation was scheduled within 120 days. Excludes legislatively negotiated trade treaties and broad multilateral agreements.

cases.name: Trump 2018 Section 232 Steel and Aluminum Tariffs
Trump 2019 Threatened Tariffs on Mexico (Immigration leverage)
Biden 2024 Chinese EV and Semiconductor Tariffs

coverage_note: 9 named; believed roughly 9 to 10 significant unilateral short-fuse tariff proclamations in modern US history.
known_gaps: Borderline cases involving subtle backroom concessions that technically paused rather than structurally blocked implementation are difficult to uniformly classify.
skeleton: Executive trade actions announced with short implementation horizons divided into those that proceeded (miss) vs those halted or delayed by structural/negotiated friction before deadline (hit). Total: 9 cases.
multiplier: 3 hits out of 9 historical instances where executive-threatened/announced tariffs faced structural or negotiated friction leading to avoidance before the deadline.
validity_reason: Executive trade authorities under statutes like Section 232, Section 301, and IEEPA remain stable over multi-year political cycles, though judicial scrutiny of executive overreach is evolving.
